title: 7 Best Log Splitters in 2026: Tonnage, Speed and Vertical Use
keywords: best wood splitters on the market
description: The Champion 27-Ton is the best log splitter for several cords a year: 27 tons, vertical and horizontal use and auto-return. Six more for every woodpile.
dek: The Champion 27-Ton is the best log splitter for several cords a year: 27 tons, vertical and horizontal use and auto-return.
intro: The best log splitter for most people who burn several cords a year is the Champion Power Equipment 27-Ton, a towable gas machine that splits horizontally or vertically and has an auto-return valve. If you only split seasoned wood for a fireplace or fire pit, a quiet 7-ton electric such as the Boss Industrial ES7T20 is the better fit.

Shoppers fixate on tonnage, but most firewood splits well within the reach of a mid-size machine. What decides how long a day at the woodpile takes is cycle time, whether you can split heavy rounds without lifting them, and whether the machine matches the number of cords you actually burn. This guide ranks seven splitters across gas, electric and manual types, then answers the sizing, tonnage and safety questions buyers search most.
quickAnswer: Buy the Champion 27-Ton if you split several cords a year, the Cub Cadet LS 27 if you want heavier construction and dealer service, and the YARDMAX YU2566 or Powerhorse 22-Ton for gas splitting on a tighter budget. For fireplace and fire pit volumes, the Boss Industrial ES7T20 or WEN 56207 electric splitters are quieter and simpler.

blocks.p: The **Champion 27-Ton** is the best log splitter for most households that heat with wood, because it pairs 27 tons with vertical operation, a two-stage pump and auto-return. The **Cub Cadet LS 27** is the build-quality upgrade, and the **Boss Industrial ES7T20** is the pick for quiet electric splitting near the house.

sections.h: The 7 Best Log Splitters in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: Picks are ranked on manufacturer specifications for splitting force, listed cycle time, maximum log length, power source, orientation and warranty, plus beam construction and the recurring themes in owner feedback. No splitting trials were run for this guide, so none of the figures below are our own measurements.

Champion's 27-ton splitter is a full-size towable gas machine that handles nearly any homeowner firewood job. It splits at waist height in horizontal mode, then tips upright so you can roll heavy, knotty rounds onto the foot plate instead of hoisting them. Champion's listing highlights a quick cycle time for the class, a two-stage hydraulic pump, a Champion engine and an auto-return valve that retracts the ram without you holding the lever. Log cradles on the beam catch split halves so they do not hit the ground between strokes, which saves a lot of bending over a full day. It tows behind a vehicle at modest speeds, and parts support is good. It is too much machine for a fire pit owner and heavier to move around a small yard than an electric, but for several cords a year it is the best balance of speed, capability and value here.
**Pros:** 27 tons with vertical and horizontal use; auto-return valve; log cradles; good parts support. **Cons:** Overkill for small volumes; loud and heavy; engine upkeep required.

blocks.h3: Best Build Quality: Cub Cadet LS 27 CCHP

blocks.p: The LS 27 is Cub Cadet's 27-ton towable gas splitter, and owners consistently describe its frame, beam and hitch as sturdier than budget rivals. It converts between horizontal and vertical operation and uses a two-stage pump with auto-return, so day-to-day it works much like the Champion. The difference is in the hardware that wears first on hard-used machines: hitches, beams and hydraulic fittings. Cub Cadet's dealer network is a real advantage if you want local service rather than mail-order parts. It usually costs more than comparable Champion or YARDMAX models, so you are paying for build and support rather than extra force. For someone who expects to split five or more cords a year for a decade, that premium makes sense. As with every towable splitter, check the maximum towing speed on the label and your state's rules on lights and registration before driving it on public roads.
**Pros:** Robust frame, beam and hitch; vertical and horizontal; two-stage pump with auto-return; dealer service. **Cons:** Priced above similar-tonnage rivals; heavy to move by hand.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cub+Cadet+LS+27+log+splitter&tag=sktiger-20)

The YU2566 brings 25 tons, full-beam construction and vertical and horizontal operation to a lower price than most name-brand gas splitters. The full beam adds rigidity, and the machine uses a two-stage pump and an auto-return valve like the more expensive picks. It tows behind a vehicle and suits owners who split a few cords a year and want gas speed without paying for a dealer-sold brand. Expect fit and finish a notch below the Cub Cadet, and plan to check hydraulic fittings and bolts after the first few hours of use, which is good practice on any new splitter. Parts and service exist but are less widespread than for the biggest brands. For buyers asking which splitter is the best value with vertical capability, this is one of the strongest answers.
**Pros:** 25 tons at a value price; full beam; vertical and horizontal; auto-return. **Cons:** Fit and finish below premium brands; smaller service network.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=YARDMAX+YU2566&tag=sktiger-20)

Powerhorse is Northern Tool's house brand, and its 22-ton splitter offers vertical and horizontal operation, a two-stage pump and auto-return for less than many 25 to 27-ton machines. For seasoned oak, maple and ash in ordinary round sizes, 22 tons is enough, so the lower rating costs you little in practice. It is a sensible machine for two or three cords a year when you want vertical capability for the occasional big round without paying for tonnage you will rarely use. Northern Tool's store network helps with parts. Where it slows down is very large, twisted or green elm and sweetgum, which is exactly where the 27-ton machines earn their premium. Check fittings after the first hours of use and keep the hydraulic fluid at the level the manual lists.
**Pros:** Vertical and horizontal for less; 22 tons covers most seasoned wood; auto-return; store parts network. **Cons:** Slower on stringy or knotty rounds; gas engine maintenance.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Powerhorse+22+ton+log+splitter&tag=sktiger-20)

The ES7T20 is a 7-ton electric splitter that plugs into a standard household outlet and, per the manufacturer, takes logs up to about 20 inches long. Electric splitters run quietly, produce no exhaust and need no engine care, so you can use one in an open garage or right next to the house without annoying the neighbors. It is aimed at modest volumes of seasoned wood for a fireplace or fire pit. Seven tons handles straight-grained seasoned rounds of moderate diameter but will stall on large, knotty or green pieces. It works horizontally only, so you lift every round onto the beam. Use the extension cord gauge and length the manual specifies, or plug straight into a GFCI outlet, and never keep cycling the ram into a round that will not split.
**Pros:** Quiet, no fumes, no engine upkeep; household outlet; fits in a garage. **Cons:** Stalls on big, knotty or green wood; horizontal only; slower than gas.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Boss+Industrial+ES7T20&tag=sktiger-20)

WEN's 56207 is an inexpensive 6.5-ton electric splitter for people who burn a little wood and are tired of swinging a maul. It runs on household current, sits on a stand or bench at a workable height and is light enough to roll around the garage. It suits seasoned, straight-grained rounds of modest diameter, the kind of wood that ends up in a backyard fire pit, and it is handy for turning larger splits into kindling. Like every small electric unit, it can stall on knots, crotches and green hardwood, and you should not force it by cycling the ram over and over. Its strength is price; its limits are speed and capacity. Owners who burn under a cord a winter may never need more.
**Pros:** Low price; light and easy to store; quiet with no fuel. **Cons:** Low tonnage stalls on knots; horizontal only; slow for larger volumes.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=WEN+56207&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Manual: Sun Joe LJ10M Logger Joe 10-Ton

blocks.p: The LJ10M is a manual hydraulic splitter: you pump the handles and a hydraulic ram drives the log into the wedge. There is no engine, motor or cord, so it works anywhere and makes almost no noise. Sun Joe rates it at 10 tons, more than the small electrics on paper, but every split takes many pump strokes, so speed is the trade. It fits a cabin with no power, a camper who wants kindling, or anyone who wants a safer alternative to a maul for small amounts of seasoned wood. It is not practical for cords. Set it on firm, level ground so it cannot tip while you pump, and keep your hands clear of the wedge even though the ram moves slowly.
**Pros:** No fuel, cord or battery; very quiet; inexpensive. **Cons:** Slow, effortful pumping; impractical for large volumes; limited log size.

sections.h: What Size Log Splitter Do You Need?

blocks.p: Size the splitter to the cords you split per year. A full cord is a stack 4 feet high, 4 feet deep and 8 feet long, or 128 cubic feet. A household burning a face cord in a fire pit needs a very different machine from one heating a house on six to eight cords.

blocks.h3: Does the type of wood change the size?

blocks.p: Yes. Seasoned, straight-grained oak, ash and maple split far more easily than green elm, sweetgum or crotch wood. If you drop and buck your own trees, you get a mix that includes stubborn pieces from the base and branch unions. Size the machine for those, not the easy rounds.

Absolutely. Hoisting rounds that weigh 60 to 100 pounds up to beam height all afternoon is brutal on the body. If big rounds are common in your pile, vertical operation stops being a nice extra and becomes the main feature.

blocks.h3: How much space does a splitter need?

blocks.p: A towable gas splitter takes roughly the footprint of a small trailer and wants a dry spot in the off-season. Electric and manual units fit on a garage shelf, which can settle the choice on a small lot.

sections.h: How Many Tons Does a Log Splitter Need?

blocks.p: For seasoned, straight-grained rounds of modest diameter, 4 to 7 tons is enough. For nearly all homeowner firewood, bigger and knottier rounds included, plan on 20 to 27 tons. Machines rated above that are built for production firewood and very large, stringy wood.

blocks.h3: What does the tonnage rating mean?

blocks.p: It is the maximum force the ram can apply, calculated from cylinder size and peak pump pressure. Brands calculate and advertise it differently, so a 25-ton machine from one maker is not automatically weaker than a 27-ton machine from another.

blocks.h3: Log splitter 21 ton vs 27 ton: which should you buy?

blocks.p: For seasoned hardwood in normal round sizes, a 21 or 22-ton splitter handles the work, and the money saved can go toward a faster cycle or vertical operation. A 27-ton machine pulls ahead on large, green or interlocked-grain wood like elm and sweetgum, and on knots and crotches. If you cut your own trees and split them green, buy the 27; if you buy seasoned cordwood, the 21 or 22 is usually enough.

No. Past a point, extra tons do not split ordinary firewood any faster. A 22-ton splitter with a quick cycle often clears a pile sooner than a 30-ton unit with a slow one. Buy enough force for your toughest regular wood, then spend the rest on speed, vertical operation and build quality.

sections.h: What Is a Good Cycle Time, and Which Features Are Worth Paying For?

blocks.p: Many gas splitters list a cycle time between about 10 and 20 seconds, and small electrics are slower. Cycle time is how long the ram takes to extend and return; across hundreds of splits, a few seconds per stroke adds up to hours.

blocks.h3: Why does a two-stage pump matter?

blocks.p: It drives the ram quickly at low pressure until it touches the wood, switches to slow high-pressure travel to split it, then speeds back up. Treat it as a must on any gas splitter.
Once the log pops, you shove the lever to return and walk away from it. A detent holds it until the ram is fully back, freeing your hands to set up the next piece.

For big rounds, more than any other feature. You roll the round onto the foot plate instead of lifting it. If you search for the best vertical/horizontal log splitter, every gas pick on this list qualifies.

blocks.h3: Do log cradles, beams and wedges matter?

blocks.p: Yes. Cradles keep split halves at beam height. Heavier I-beams flex less than light channel beams. Some machines accept a four-way wedge that quarters a round in one pass, which speeds up stove-size splitting on straight wood, though it needs more force on knotty pieces.

blocks.h3: What should you check on a towable model?

blocks.p: Hitch type, tire size and the maximum towing speed on the label. Many splitters are not built for highway speeds.
Brands measure cycle times under different conditions, so use them to compare machines within a class rather than across brands.

sections.h: Gas, Electric or Manual: Which Type Should You Buy?

blocks.p: Go with gas when your yearly total tops a cord or two or your pile holds big-diameter rounds. Choose electric for small volumes of seasoned wood when quiet and simplicity matter. Manual and kinetic splitters serve narrower needs.

Expect roughly 4 to 10 tons, horizontal operation and slower cycles. They are quiet enough for the garage, need almost no maintenance and suit seasoned wood. Use the cord the manual calls for.

A manual splitter uses a hand-pumped jack, so it needs no power at all but takes many strokes per log. A kinetic splitter stores energy in a heavy flywheel and drives the ram very quickly, which is fast but demands extra caution.

Brand matters less than tonnage class, vertical capability, pump design and the service network near you. Compare the same tonnage side by side on cycle time, beam construction, warranty and parts availability, then pick the one with a better local support story.

sections.h: How Do You Use a Log Splitter Safely?

blocks.p: One person runs the machine, and nobody's hands go near the ram or wedge while either is moving. The ram delivers tons of force and will not stop for a finger.

When one person loads and another works the lever, the operator cannot see exactly where the loader's hands are. Manufacturers warn against two-person operation, and it is a leading cause of crushed hands. Helpers should stack splits well clear of the machine.

On the sides of the log to position it, then off the log entirely before you engage the control. Never reposition a log or clear a jam while the ram is moving or under pressure, and never split two logs at once.

Never run a hand along a hose to find a leak. Fluid escaping from a pinhole under pressure can be injected through skin, an injury that needs emergency surgical care. Use a piece of cardboard to locate a leak and relieve pressure before touching fittings.

Safety glasses, snug gloves, protective-toe boots, long pants and hearing protection around gas engines. Skip loose sleeves, drawstrings and jewelry. Set the machine on firm, level ground with the wheels chocked.

blocks.h3: Can you run a gas splitter in a garage?

blocks.p: No. Gas engines produce carbon monoxide, which builds fast in enclosed spaces even with the door open. Run gas splitters outdoors only, and refuel with the engine off and cool. For splitting next to the house, an electric unit is the safer choice.

sections.h: How Do You Split, Season and Maintain Firewood Gear?

blocks.p: Cut rounds to one consistent length that fits both your stove and the splitter's maximum log length, often 16 to 20 inches for wood stoves. Square, flat cuts sit steady on the beam. Aim the wedge along existing checks and away from knots.

Halve or quarter the big rounds first, then turn those pieces into stove-length splits. A [hookaroon](/best-hookaroon-reviews/) lets you drag rounds and toss splits without bending, which adds up over several cords. Stack as you go so you handle each piece once. If you move logs around a larger property, a [compact tractor](/best-compact-tractor/) with pallet forks does the heavy hauling.

blocks.h3: How long does firewood take to season?

blocks.p: Plan on six months at minimum for hardwood, and a full year or longer is common. The US EPA's Burn Wise program recommends 20 percent moisture or less for clean burning. Stack splits off the ground in a sunny, breezy spot with the top covered and the sides open, and check with an inexpensive moisture meter. Keep weeds and brush trimmed around the stacks with a [string trimmer](/best-weed-eater/) so air can move and pests have less cover.

blocks.h3: How do you maintain a log splitter?

blocks.p: Check hydraulic fluid before every session and change fluid and filter at the hours the manual lists. Inspect hoses and replace damaged ones rather than patching them. On gas units, change the engine oil after break-in and on schedule, keep the air filter clean and use fresh, stabilized fuel. Grease the beam and ram guides, dress burrs off the wedge, and check bolts, the hitch and tire pressure. Electric units mostly need clean motor vents, a fluid check and indoor storage.

If you only split a cord or two once a year, renting makes sense; cut and stack the rounds before you collect the machine so the rental clock is not wasted. Buy if you split every year. Typical retail pricing runs from low hundreds of dollars for manual and small electric units to low thousands for mid-size gas splitters, so sharing a gas machine with a neighbor is a popular middle path.

mistakes: Nearly all homeowner firewood splits within the reach of a 20 to 27-ton gas machine, and extra tons rarely speed anything up. Cycle time, a two-stage pump and auto-return decide how long your pile takes. Buy enough force for your toughest regular wood and spend the rest on features.

One person loading while another works the lever is a classic way to crush fingers, because the operator cannot see where the other person's hands are. Manufacturers warn against it. The same person should place the log and run the control, with helpers stacking well away.
Lifting heavy rounds onto the beam

Repeatedly lifting heavy rounds to beam height leads to sore backs and logs landing on toes. If large rounds are part of your pile, buy a splitter with vertical operation and roll heavy pieces onto the foot plate. A hookaroon moves them into place without bending.
Running a gas splitter in a garage

Gas engines produce carbon monoxide, which is invisible, odorless and builds quickly in enclosed spaces even with the door open. Run gas splitters outdoors only, away from doors and windows. If you need to split right beside the house, choose an electric model.
Feeling for hydraulic leaks by hand

A pinhole leak in a pressurized line can inject fluid through skin, an injury that needs emergency treatment even when it looks minor. Find leaks with cardboard, relieve pressure before loosening fittings, and replace damaged hoses instead of wrapping or patching them.
bottomLine: For anyone burning several cords a year, the Champion 27-Ton is the best log splitter for the money, balancing 27 tons, vertical operation and a fast auto-return cycle. Step up to the Cub Cadet LS 27 for sturdier construction and dealer support, save with the YARDMAX YU2566 or Powerhorse 22-Ton, and choose the Boss ES7T20 or WEN 56207 electrics for fire pit and fireplace wood. Whatever you buy, run it alone, keep your hands off the log while the ram moves, never test for leaks with your skin, keep gas engines outdoors and season the wood to 20 percent moisture before you burn it.

faqs.q: What is the best log splitter?
faqs.a: The Champion Power Equipment 27-Ton is the best log splitter for most households that burn several cords a year, combining 27 tons, vertical and horizontal operation, a two-stage pump and auto-return. Buyers who want sturdier construction and dealer service should choose the Cub Cadet LS 27, and fire pit owners are better served by a quiet electric.

faqs.q: What are the best and most reliable 26 ton log splitters?
faqs.a: In the 25 to 27-ton class, the Cub Cadet LS 27 has the strongest reputation for durable frames, beams and hitches, and the Champion 27-Ton offers the best mix of speed and value. The YARDMAX YU2566 is the budget 25-ton option. Reliability depends heavily on fluid checks, fresh fuel and covered storage.

faqs.q: Log splitter 21 ton vs 27 ton: is the bigger one worth it?
faqs.a: For seasoned hardwood in ordinary sizes, a 21 or 22-ton splitter does the job and costs less. A 27-ton machine is worth it if you split green wood, very large rounds, knots or stringy species like elm and sweetgum. Cycle time and vertical operation matter as much as the extra tons.

faqs.q: Is an electric log splitter good enough?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as you are splitting seasoned wood in fireplace or fire pit quantities. Electric splitters such as the Boss ES7T20 are quiet, produce no fumes and need little maintenance. They cycle slower than gas, work horizontally only and stall on large, knotty or green rounds. If you split more than a cord or two a year, choose gas.

faqs.q: What is the best value vertical capable wood splitter?
faqs.a: The YARDMAX YU2566 and the Powerhorse 22-Ton are the best values with vertical operation. The YARDMAX adds a full beam and 25 tons, while the Powerhorse saves more money and still handles most seasoned firewood. Both use a two-stage pump and auto-return, the two features that make gas splitters fast.

faqs.q: How long should firewood season after splitting?
faqs.a: Give hardwood six months at a minimum, often a year or more, in a raised stack that gets sun and wind, with a cover on top and open sides. The EPA Burn Wise program recommends 20 percent moisture or less, and a cheap moisture meter tells you when the wood has reached it.

faqs.q: Should I rent a log splitter instead of buying one?
faqs.a: Rent if you split once a year and handle a cord or two, and have the wood cut and staged before you pick the machine up. If you split every year or work through several cords at a time, buying usually pays for itself within a few seasons, especially if neighbors share the cost.
